subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext: Does he agree with Senator Roebuck, Senator Gouin who, I think, was on the committee, and several other very distinguished lawyers that a draft such as the one I have placed before the house today should be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada for its decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, having regard to the fact there was nothing in my hon. friend's last speech and nothing in his resolution to indicate he was going to submit an argument of this sort, I must say in all candour that I have never considered it. It is a matter upon which I would not want to express an opinion unless I had considered it carefully because I think there is nothing more unhelpful in a matter of this kind than the expression of unconsidered opinions.
My hon. friend, amongst other things, wants an assurance of freedom of religion. I suggest that we have freedom of religion in Canada right now. We have every kind and description of religion. Each sect practises its religion in any way it chooses, and none is barred unless in the course of practising its religion it breaks the law of the land. Let us, for example, take an extreme hypothetical case, and I am taking this case because there are no examples of it. I could take cases of a religion concerning which people who believe in that religion have been found guilty under the Criminal Code of not providing necessaries for those who were dependent upon them, but I am taking this other case because there are no examples of it and therefore it will not give any offence.
Let us take a religion that offered up human sacrifices, which at one time in the world's history was a practice of some religions. I have no doubt that there would be a general desire to have the offering of human sacrifices prohibited by law, not as an interference with freedom of religion but merely to stamp out a practice which was

Human Rights
disapproved by an overwhelming majority of Canadian citizens. Now, sir, I know of no constitutional amendment which would protect a Canadian citizen who had, for example, for religious reasons offered a human sacrifice of this sort. There is no protection that would interfere with the visitation of a penalty upon him.
I would point out that all constitutional guarantees must be interpreted by the courts, and the court in this hypothetical case I have mentioned-

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext: But the hypothetical case would not concern freedom. The United States supreme court dealt with the point and said there is no freedom in an action such as the minister contemplates. That is exactly the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext: That is right. I agree with my hon. friend.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext: The minister is raising a straw man.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext: In a case of that sort the court would hear the evidence and would have to decide upon the evidence adduced in the case before it whether in substance what the accused had done was to practise freedom of religion or to break the law against human sacrifices. If the courts of any country in which these constitutional guarantees exist find that what has happened is that human sacrifices have been offered, the existence of the constitutional guarantees in favour of religious freedom would not protect the person charged.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext: I would hope not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext:
My hon. friend may not agree with the judgments of the courts in certain cases because, like the hon. member, myself and all members of the house, judges are human beings and like all of us they are fallible. That is why we have courts of appeal, and the courts of appeal are also fallible. But does the hon. member think that by a bill of rights we can make judges infallible or that we can protect ourselves against the human fallibility of judges who have to interpret these bills of rights?
My hon. friend mentioned freedom of speech. Well, sir, I should have thought that we have a very great measure of freedom of speech in this country. I can recall my hon. friend's own leader and several of his colleagues, who were very voluble in the former parliament and in the election campaigns of 1949 and 1953, supporting the thesis with resounding eloquence that the communists of this country enjoyed far too much freedom of speech and freedom of the press, and that this government was derelict in its duty for not taking steps to curtail the 
freedom of speech of these gentlemen, or perhaps to curtail their freedom of movement, or perhaps to curtail their freedom- period. Now at that time my hon. friend's thesis was that there was too much freedom. Today, he says there is too little. His arguments oscillate with time and place.
My hon. friend wants to guarantee freedom of the press. Well, sir, I should like him to tell us, if he will, what freedom of the press it is that is not now available to the newspaper and other publishers of this country. During the last parliament his colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), introduced a bill which we all supported to interfere with the freedom of the press with regard to obscene publications and crime comics. Was it not proper that we should have done so? If we had a constitutional amendment guaranteeing freedom of the press, there might be some question although I think properly interpreted there would not be. But at least I think this is a case in which we can trust the good judgment of parliament.
If my hon. friend can think of any example of a curtailment of the freedom of the press would he not, upon reflection, agree that it could be removed by either a provincial enactment or a federal enactment, depending upon whether the particular case fell under federal or provincial jurisdiction? It is not so very long ago, and the hon. member for Prince Albert brought this matter up this afternoon, when one of the provincial legislatures passed a law which, as we could see this afternoon, offended my hon. friend's views as to the degree of freedom which the press should have in this country. What happened? Action was taken in the courts, the same courts that would be interpreting a bill of rights-

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext: If the minister would allow me to correct him, I would say that action was not taken. The dominion government was asked to disallow that enactment, but they did not disallow it. It was submitted, then, to the supreme court. No action was taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite correct.
I was referring to that, improperly, as an action.
The matter came before the court. This was the same court which, now being the final court of appeal, would interpret any bill of rights we would have in this country. It was there held that under the present law of Canada the freedom of the press in that province could not be curtailed in the manner proposed by the legislature of the province. This happened under the present law.

Another point which my hon. friend from Prince Albert makes is that habeas corpus should not be abrogated or suspended except by parliament. I suggest that no one can name a single case in which habeas corpus has been abrogated or suspended in Canada except under the authority of parliament. Under our existing law habeas corpus is available to every subject who wishes to invoke it, and the only way it can be rendered unavailable is by an act of the appropriate legislative body which, in certain cases, is the parliament of Canada and in other cases is the provincial legislature.
When my hon. friend speaks of orders in council having done this or orders in council having done that, surely he must remember that every order in council which is used for any purpose by either the governor in council at Ottawa or by the lieutenant governors in council in the provinces, is open to challenge in the courts of this country. If a lieutenant governor in council or the governor general in council has passed an order in council which is not properly authorized by statute, no action can take place under it and the effect of any such action can be and will be quashed if it is challenged in the courts. So far as the necessity for a bill of rights to protect habeas corpus is concerned, I would submit it is not essential in any respect.
In the third paragraph of his resolution, the hon. member says:
That no one shall be deprived of liberty or property without due process of law, and in no case by order in council.
I wonder if my hon. friend realizes the extent to which a literal application of this portion of his resolution would go. Does he mean_ to say that municipalities could not exercise any of their functions which they exercise under authority delegated to them by provincial legislatures, except by due process of law?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext: That is the only way they can act, by due process of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT AS TO JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Quite. My horn, friend does not mean that they should have to have due process of law. Does he mean that we could not use an order in council to affect property? He says, "in no case by order in council". Would he think it was necessary for us in this chamber to pass a statute in every case in which the government of Canada was going to acquire any property? That is what his language states. Surely my hon. friend is quite aware of the fact this government cannot by order in council do any of the things with which my hon. friend charged it in a number of
Human Rights
the details he cited this afternoon, except under the authority of some statute of this parliament or, in very exceptional cases, under the royal prerogative. All of those cases which he cited as based on an order in council, and which he seemed to suggest had some measure of illegality or impropriety about them, could be successfully challenged by my hon. friend acting for a client if those orders in council were not properly authorized by a proper statute of parliament.
It is on the basis of such arguments as these that the hon. member wishes us to believe that in 1955 he and others who are again urging this bill of rights have seen a light which Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir George Cartier, Hon. Edward Blake, Sir Oliver Mowat, Sir John Thompson, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, Sir Allen Aylesworth, Sir Robert Borden, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, Sir L. Gouin, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, the Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent and the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley have all failed to see in their time. Perhaps he is right and they have all been wrong, but for my part I think that is improbable. The fact is, as has been accurately and succinctly stated by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), that the basic freedoms are more highly regarded and more secure to the individual in Canada than in any other country in the world with the possible exception of Great Britain.
Why are they secure? Because they are protected by the British principle of the sovereignty of parliament. It is this British principle which the hon. member for Prince Albert proposes to abridge by attaching constitutional limitations to it in the manner of the bill of rights in the United States constitution.
My hon. friend speaks for the Conservative party in this matter. Why then, may I ask him, do he and his party not believe and advocate that we should conserve what has worked well? Why do they not advocate that we should keep our meddling with the Canadian constitution to an absolute minimum? What kind of conservatism is this? Can the hon. member, looking around the world, name a single country in which a bill of rights such as he advocates has worked as well as the sovereignty of parliament has worked in both the United Kingdom and in Canada? It is a strange kind of conservatism that attempts to discard that which has worked well and to replace it with something which, wherever it has been tried has not worked nearly so well as the principle of the sovereignty of parliament in this country.

Human Rights
I have attempted to discuss all the main arguments of the mover of the resolution.
I must say, in all frankness, that if we were going to consider a bill of rights in this country I would prefer at least the language of the proposal made and standing in the name of the hon. member for Kosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I would be glad to discuss the proposal he has suggested and to indicate the methods by which I think it would have to be introduced, if introduced at all. But I would think it would be much preferable to do that after having had the benefit of a fuller expression of his views. For that reason I think I should bring my present remarks to a close.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I approach this particular topic with a good deal of trepidation, stepping in where angels fear to tread. I am not a lawyer. Certainly I am not a constitutional lawyer, and I hojie to demonstrate that by speaking more briefly than either of the two hon. gentlemen who have preceded me.
The hon. member for Prince Albert in introducing his motion this afternoon said he hoped there would be an opportunity for a vote on the proposal for the writing into our constitution of a bill of rights. With that of course I want to agree immediately. I did not know, when the hon. member rose to speak, that he was going to incorporate in his speech, though not in his resolution, the points made and the proposals suggested by the committee set up in the other place.
The motion I put on the order paper originally and which the house was good enough to allow me to withdraw this afternoon, spells out what I think should be a satisfactory bill of rights for this country. I am going to say immediately that while that resolution is in my name and was discussed with me very thoroughly, I had some of the best constitutional and legal advice in the country before I drafted it and placed it on the order paper. And I believe that is the kind of thing upon which the vote should be taken. Previous to this afternoon the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) told me that if I moved my resolution he would be glad to let his stand, and would be prepared to second what I had moved. What I am going to do this afternoon is move the substance of my motion as an amendment to the motion of the hon. member for Prince Albert. Then if the hon. member for Spadina will allow me, I shall add his name as seconder of the amendment, despite the reference made by the minister to a statement he made in a previous debate.
If I have that consent-and I understand I have-in a moment I shall move in the
[Mr. Garson.l
form of an amendment the motion which stood in my name. I think the need for explicit amendments was substantiated in several of the instances to which my hon. friend from Prince Albert referred this afternoon. And if I may say so, his reference to the religious case which was before the supreme court, and upon which there was a difference of opinion among the judges, indicates the futility of making a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada such as is suggested in the main motion, without having something far more specific than the motion indicates.
I say further that it is the duty of this parliament, representing all the people of Canada, to decide whether or not we shall have a bill of rights written into our constitution. It is not therefore the function of the supreme court to decide; it is the function of this parliament to decide.
So, as indicated, I move:
That the resolution be amended by striking out all the words after the words "advisability of" in the preamble of the resolution, and substituting therefor the following:
"The taking of whatever steps are necessary to amend the British North America Act so as to include therein the following headings and sections:
